claim: The brain uses an internal model of the body to predict the consequences of motor commands before sensory feedback arrives.
source: It is thought that the brain does not simply react to sensory feedback, but rather uses an internal model of the body to predict the consequences of motor commands before sensory feedback arrives.
evidence: This is a statement about established theory in motor control, drawing from general scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Time-delayed sensory feedback can be used to correct for perturbations, motor noise, or a moving target.
source: Time-delayed sensory feedback can then be used to correct for the unexpected—perturbations, motor noise, or a moving target.
evidence: This is a statement about established understanding of sensory feedback function in motor control.

claim: The cerebellum has been implicated in predictive control processes.
source: The cerebellum has been implicated in this predictive control process.
evidence: This statement references prior research implicating the cerebellum in prediction, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: The feedback gain in patients with cerebellar ataxia matches that of healthy subjects.
source: Here, we show that the feedback gain in patients with cerebellar ataxia matches that of healthy subjects, but that patients exhibit substantially more phase lag.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiment 1 showing similar scaling factors between patients and controls.

claim: Cerebellar ataxia patients exhibit substantially more phase lag than healthy subjects.
source: Here, we show that the feedback gain in patients with cerebellar ataxia matches that of healthy subjects, but that patients exhibit substantially more phase lag.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiments 1 and 2 showing increased phase lag in patients.

claim: The difference between patients and controls is captured by a computational model incorporating a Smith predictor in healthy subjects that is missing in patients.
source: This difference is captured by a computational model incorporating a Smith predictor in healthy subjects that is missing in patients, supporting the predictive role of the cerebellum in feedback control.
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results presented in the manuscript, specifically the model selection procedure and comparison of model structures.

claim: Altering (phase advancing) visual feedback improves cerebellar patients' movement control in a simplified virtual reality setup.
source: Lastly, we improve cerebellar patients' movement control by altering (phase advancing) the visual feedback they receive from their own self movement in a simplified virtual reality setup.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiment 3 showing reduced dysmetria with acceleration-dependent feedback.

claim: Proprioceptive and visual feedback are necessary for determining body postures at the beginning and end of a movement.
source: Proprioceptive and visual feedback are necessary for determining body postures at the beginning and end of a movement and can be used to guide slow movements accurately.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about the role of sensory feedback in motor control.

claim: Feedback is time delayed and never represents the current state of the body during movement.
source: However, feedback is time delayed, and thus it never represents the current state of the body during movement.
evidence: This is a well-established principle in sensorimotor neuroscience.

claim: Internal models can be rapidly accessed and provide a fast internal prediction system to estimate how a movement will unfold.
source: These models can be rapidly accessed and thus provide a fast internal prediction system to estimate how a movement will unfold, enabling us to better understand where our limbs are at any given moment.
evidence: This statement describes the theoretical function of internal models in motor control, representing established knowledge.

claim: Internal models allow us to make fast and accurate movements despite long-latency feedback.
source: This allows us to make fast and accurate movements despite long-latency feedback.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about the function of internal models, representing established knowledge in motor control.

claim: People with cerebellar damage show a characteristic pattern of incoordination during movement referred to as ataxia.
source: People with cerebellar damage show a characteristic pattern of incoordination during movement that is referred to as ataxia.
evidence: This is a well-established clinical observation about cerebellar damage.

claim: When reaching, cerebellar patients make curved movements that miss intended targets and require multiple corrections.
source: When reaching, they make curved movements that miss intended targets and require multiple corrections.
evidence: This describes a well-documented clinical feature of cerebellar ataxia.

claim: Dysmetria and intention tremor are hallmarks of cerebellar ataxia.
source: This pattern of over- and undershooting a target (dysmetria) and oscillatory corrections (intention tremor) are hallmarks of cerebellar ataxia.
evidence: This describes well-established clinical features of cerebellar ataxia.

claim: One hypothesis for ataxia is that the predictive estimation and control provided by cerebellar circuits is dysfunctional or lost.
source: One hypothesis that might explain ataxia is that the predictive estimation and control provided by cerebellar circuits is dysfunctional or lost (Miall et al., 2007; Wolpert et al., 1998).
evidence: This hypothesis is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Estimation of limb state normally benefits from integrating proprioceptive measurements with an internal predictive control model during a movement.
source: Normally, the estimation of limb state (e.g. position and velocity) benefits from integrating proprioceptive measurements with an internal predictive control model during a movement (Adamovich et al., 1998; Fuentes and Bastian, 2010; Paillard and Brouchon, 1974).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Patients with cerebellar damage do not receive the benefit of integrating proprioceptive measurements with an internal predictive control model.
source: However, patients with cerebellar damage do not seem to receive this benefit (Bhanpuri et al., 2013; Weeks et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The predictive model in cerebellar patients may convey incorrect state information during active movements, corrupting proprioceptive estimation of limb state.
source: Worse, it is possible that their predictive model actually conveys incorrect state information during active movements, which could corrupt rather than enhance proprioceptive estimation of limb state.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about a possible mechanism underlying cerebellar deficits.

claim: Difficulty predicting the future state of limbs during active movement leads to movements that are poorly directed and scaled, requiring ongoing corrections.
source: This difficulty of predicting the future state of limbs during active movement leads to movements that are poorly directed and scaled, requiring ongoing corrections to reach a goal location.
evidence: This is an inference about the consequences of impaired prediction in cerebellar patients.

claim: Patients with cerebellar ataxia may rely more heavily on visual feedback to correct dysmetric movements.
source: Patients with cerebellar ataxia may rely more heavily on visual feedback to correct dysmetric movements (Beppu et al., 1987; Beppu et al., 1984; Day et al., 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Visual feedback is slower than proprioception.
source: A drawback of visual feedback is that it is slower than proprioception
evidence: This is established knowledge about sensory processing speeds.

claim: Intention tremor in cerebellar patients is thought to stem from dependence on time-delayed visual feedback to make corrections.
source: intention tremor in these patients' movements is thought to stem from dependence on time-delayed visual feedback to make corrections (Day et al., 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: A gait study by Morton and Bastian suggested that cerebellar patients could use feedback information to make reactive corrections during split-belt treadmill walking but lacked the ability to adapt their predictive motor patterns.
source: A gait study by Morton and Bastian suggested that cerebellar patients could use feedback information to make reactive corrections during split-belt treadmill walking in order to maintain stability, but lacked the ability to adapt their predictive motor patterns (Morton and Bastian, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Other studies have indirectly supported the notion that patients can incorporate some level of visual feedback control in reaching.
source: Other studies have indirectly supported the notion that patients can incorporate some level of visual feedback control in reaching (Day et al., 1998; Smith et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Cerebellar patients can integrate visual feedback control similarly to healthy, age-matched control subjects.
source: This method allowed us to determine that cerebellar patients can integrate visual feedback control similarly to healthy, age-matched control subjects.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiment 1 showing similar scaling factors.

claim: Providing an acceleration-dependent alteration to visual feedback of a hand cursor compensates for phase lags introduced by time delay.
source: Specifically, we provided an acceleration-dependent alteration to visual feedback of a hand cursor. This alteration serves to compensate for the phase lags introduced by time delay, allowing patients to use visual feedback more effectively.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about the mechanism of the intervention, supported by the experimental results.

claim: The real-time controller successfully reduced patients' dysmetria.
source: This real-time controller successfully reduced patients' dysmetria.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiment 3.

claim: A total of 17 patients with cerebellar deficits and 14 age-matched controls were tested in one or more experiments.
source: A total of 17 patients with cerebellar deﬁcits and 14 age-matched controls were tested in one or more of the following experiments.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study population.

claim: Patients were excluded if they had any clinical or MRI evidence of damage to extra-cerebellar brain structures.
source: Patients were excluded if they had any clinical or MRI evidence of damage to extra-cerebellar brain structures, or clinical evidence of dementia, aphasia, peripheral vestibular loss, or sensory neuropathy.
evidence: This describes the exclusion criteria for the study.

claim: Experiments 1–2 tested 11 cerebellar patients and 11 age-matched controls.
source: Experiments 1–2 tested 11 cerebellar patients (seven male, four female) and 11 age-matched controls (four male, seven female).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental participants.

claim: Experiment 3 tested 12 cerebellar patients and 12 age-matched controls.
source: Experiment 3 tested 12 cerebellar patients (eight male, four female) and 12 age-matched controls (three male, nine female)
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental participants.

claim: The KINARM system exhibits a cursor delay of 0.0458 s.
source: Using a high-speed camera, we measured this delay (0.0458 s) and took the delay into account in modeling the human control system.
evidence: This is a measurement of the experimental apparatus delay.

claim: The target trajectory comprised 15 sine waves whose frequencies were prime multiples of 0.05 Hz.
source: The target trajectory comprised 15 sine waves whose frequencies were prime multiples of 0.05 Hz, namely 0.1, 0.15, 0.25, 0.35, 0.55, 0.65, 0.85, 0.95, 1.15, 1.45, 1.55, 1.85, 2.05, 2.15, and 2.35 Hz.
evidence: This describes the experimental stimulus design.

claim: The non-harmonic relation of the component sinusoids created a temporally complex target motion that repeats every 20 s.
source: The non-harmonic relation of the component sinusoids created a temporally complex target motion with 45 degrees of freedom (amplitude, phase, and frequency for 15 sinusoids) that repeats every 20 s
evidence: This describes a property of the experimental stimulus design.

claim: The complexity and long period of the sum-of-sines signal makes the target motion far less predictable than a simple single-sine motion.
source: This complexity, coupled with the long period, makes this target motion far less predictable than a simple single-sine motion (Miall and Jackson, 2006; Poulton, 1974; Roth et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research and describes a property of the stimulus design.

claim: The dramatic increase in tracking phase lag for sum-of-sine responses recapitulates the main finding of Roth et al., 2011.
source: Lastly, the dramatic increase in tracking phase lag presented in this paper (see Results) for sum-of-sine responses recapitulates the main finding of Roth et al., 2011, confirming that from a practical point of view subjects were less able to predict the movement trajectories.
evidence: This statement compares the current results to prior research findings.

claim: Both groups scaled up or scaled down their movement commensurate with the respective decrease or increase of the cursor Feedback Gain.
source: Both groups scaled up (patients: p=0.03, t = −2.1, DOF = 10; controls: p=4×10−6, t = −8.3, DOF = 10) or scaled down (patients: p=0.005, t = 3.23, DOF = 10; controls p=0.0002, t = 5.3, DOF = 10) their movement, commensurate with the respective decrease or increase of the cursor Feedback Gain.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 1.

claim: The effect of Feedback Gain on Scaling Factor was significant.
source: We performed a two-way ANOVA, confirming that the effect of Feedback Gain (0.65 vs. 1.35) on Scaling Factor was significant (F(1,40)=59.7, p=2×10−9, ηp2=0.7)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The effect of group (patient vs. control) on Scaling Factor was not significant.
source: whereas the effect of group (patient vs. control) on Scaling Factor was not significant (F(1,40)=0.05, p=0.83)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: There was no significant interaction between group and gain on Scaling Factor.
source: with no significant interaction between group and gain (F(1,40)=3.57, p=0.07).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Subjects typically exhibited a Scaling Factor of around 1.2 in the 1.35 Feedback Gain condition.
source: Note that the subjects typically exhibited a Scaling Factor of around 1.2 in the 1.35 Feedback Gain condition.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: For a Feedback Gain of 0.65, the Scaling Factor was typically approximately 0.8.
source: Likewise, for a Feedback Gain of 0.65, the Scaling Factor was typically approximately 0.8
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The patients' responses to the feedback scaling were comparable to that of age-matched controls, suggesting that they were able to use visual feedback in a substantively similar manner.
source: Critically, the patients' responses to the feedback scaling were comparable to that of age-matched controls, suggesting that they were able to use visual feedback in a substantively similar manner.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results from Experiment 1.

claim: Visual Delays for controls were found to be 141–147 ms in the top four models.
source: In the four top models, Visual Delays for controls were found to be 141–147 ms, which is physiologically plausible.
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling results.

claim: Patients exhibited Visual Delays of 181–211 ms in the top four models.
source: Interestingly, this delay was much shorter than for patients, whose Visual Delays were 181–211 ms.
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling results.

claim: Patients exhibited longer response delay both on the visual measurement of target motion and that of self-movement feedback, compared to controls.
source: Critically, patients exhibited longer response delay both on the visual measurement of target motion and that of self-movement feedback, compared to controls.
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling results.

claim: Visual Gain values are all approximately 0.40 in the top models.
source: Visual Gain values are all approximately 0.40 which also seems reasonable given a visual inspection of the data: subjects do not appear to be attempting to replicate the full magnitude of the signal, but some smaller portion of the signal.
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling results and visual inspection of data.

claim: Patients exhibited substantially greater phase lag at high frequencies than controls.
source: Patients exhibited substantially greater phase lag at high frequencies than controls
evidence: This is an observation from the frequency response analysis.

claim: At low frequencies, both populations exhibited very little phase lag, but controls exhibited slightly more phase lag than patients.
source: at low frequencies, both populations exhibited very little phase lag, but, surprisingly, controls exhibited slightly more phase lag than patients in this frequency range.
evidence: This is an observation from the frequency response analysis.

claim: There was a phase 'cross over' frequency between patients and controls.
source: Thus, there was a phase 'cross over' frequency between patients and controls, which was also captured by our top models
evidence: This is an observation from the frequency response analysis that was also captured by the models.

claim: At the five lowest frequencies tested, all control responses landed in/on the effort/error tradeoff circle, whereas only 31% of patient responses landed in/on the circle.
source: At the five lowest frequencies tested, all control responses landed in/on the circle, whereas only 31% of patient responses landed in/on the circle (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of the phasor plot data shown in Figure 5.

claim: 70% of patient responses exhibited larger error magnitude than the respective age-matched control responses.
source: Additionally, patients generated larger tracking errors: 70% of patient responses exhibited larger error magnitude than the respective age-matched control responses.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experimental data.

claim: Controls were significantly better than patients at single-sines tracking with 10 out of 11 controls performing better than their age-matched counterpart.
source: When we compared the difference between the aggregate tracking errors for each patient/control pair to 0, controls were significantly better than patients at single-sines tracking with 10 out of 11 controls performing better than their age-matched counterpart (p=0.012).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: For the five lowest frequencies tested in the sum-of-sines condition, 72% of control responses and 64% of patient responses were in/on the effort/error tradeoff circle.
source: for the five lowest frequencies tested in the sum-of-sines condition, 72% of control responses and 64% of patient responses were in/on the circle.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experimental data.

claim: 73% of individual patient frequency responses were more phase lagged than the responses of the age-matched control.
source: Specifically, 73% of individual patient frequency responses were more phase lagged than the responses of the age-matched control (as computed on an individual frequency basis).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experimental data.

claim: 93% of controls' and 75% of patients' tracking errors were reduced in the single-sine task in comparison to performance in the sum-of-sines task.
source: 93% of controls' and 75% of patients' tracking errors were reduced in the single-sine task in comparison to his or her performance in the sum-of-sines task.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experimental data.

claim: Patients and controls were better at tracking single-sines than sum-of-sines, with all patients and all controls having less tracking error for single-sines than sum-of-sines.
source: We then used a two-sided sign test to determine that patients (p=9×10−4) and controls (p=9×10−4) were better at tracking single-sines than sum-of-sines, with all patients and all controls having less tracking error for single-sines than sum-of-sines.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The cerebellar group had greater phase lags compared to controls in the single-sine condition.
source: Circular ANOVA for the single-sine condition showed that the cerebellar group had greater lags compared to controls (Group effect, p=1×10−8)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Phase lags increased with frequency in the single-sine condition.
source: that the lags increased with frequency (Frequency effect, p=7×10−11)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: There was an interaction such that the cerebellar group lags increased more than controls across frequency in the single-sine condition.
source: and an interaction such that the cerebellar group lags increased more than controls across frequency (Interaction effect, p=2×10−6).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The cerebellar group showed greater phase lags compared to controls in the sum-of-sines condition.
source: Overall the cerebellar group showed greater phase lags compared to controls (Group effect, p=0.02)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: There was a statistically significant effect of Frequency on phase lag in the sum-of-sines condition.
source: and there was a statistically significant effect of Frequency (Frequency effect, p=7×10−30).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Group x Frequency interaction on phase lag was less significant in the sum-of-sines condition than in the single-sine condition.
source: Group x Frequency interaction (Interaction effect, p=0.03), was less significant than that seen in the single-sine condition.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Positive Acceleration-Dependent Feedback Gain made patients more hypermetric and negative Acceleration-Dependent Feedback Gain made patients more hypometric.
source: Critically, positive Acceleration-Dependent Feedback Gain made patients more hypermetric and negative Acceleration-Dependent Feedback Gain made patients more hypometric; likewise for control subjects.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiment 3.

claim: Subject-specific Acceleration-Dependent Feedback Gain was needed to best reduce dysmetria.
source: Thus, subject-specific Acceleration-Dependent Feedback Gain was needed to best reduce dysmetria.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results showing variability in optimal gains across subjects.

claim: Increased Acceleration-Dependent Feedback Gain magnitude was needed to ameliorate greater dysmetria.
source: In general, increased Acceleration-Dependent Feedback Gain magnitude was needed to ameliorate greater dysmetria.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Cerebellar patients can use visual feedback control in a manner similar to control subjects.
source: We found that cerebellar patients can use visual feedback control in a manner similar to control subjects.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental results from Experiment 1.

claim: The patient and control models differed substantively in their feedback delay.
source: Our modeling corroborated this finding: the structure and parameters between patients and controls were generally the same, except that the patient and control models differed substantively in their feedback delay.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling analysis.

claim: The patients relied on time delayed cursor feedback of their hand position, whereas controls appeared to be able to generate predictions of their hand position.
source: The patients relied on time delayed cursor feedback of their hand position, whereas controls appeared to be able to generate predictions of their hand position.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the modeling results.

claim: Cerebellar patients could leverage their intact, albeit delayed, feedback control ability to improve their movement when visual feedback is manipulated to assist them.
source: Indeed, we found that cerebellar patients could leverage their intact, albeit delayed, feedback control ability to improve their movement when we manipulate their visual feedback to assist them.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental results from Experiment 3.

claim: Cerebellar patients are thought to make faulty state estimates of arm motion due to a damaged internal model.
source: Cerebellar patients are thought to make faulty state estimates of arm motion due to a damaged internal model, which adversely affects their proprioceptive estimates during active movement (Bhanpuri et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Healthy subjects normally rely more on proprioception than vision for feedback control.
source: This hypothesis is supported by work that showed that healthy subjects normally rely more on proprioception than vision for feedback control (Crevecoeur et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Increased variability of proprioceptive information would lead to increased weighting of visual feedback.
source: Based on the Crevecoeur et al., 2016 model, increased variability of the proprioceptive information would lead to increased weighting of visual feedback (Crevecoeur et al., 2016; Weeks et al., 2017)
evidence: This statement is based on inference from cited prior research.

claim: Healthy controls can make corrections for current target movements based on a prediction of the present limb state from outdated measurements and known motor commands.
source: In other words, healthy controls can make corrections for current target movements based on a prediction of the present limb state from outdated measurements and known motor commands, rather than waiting on delayed sensory feedback.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the modeling results showing negligible feedback delay in controls.

claim: Some patients with cerebellar damage exhibit longer than usual reaction time delays when asked to make discrete, rapid movements.
source: Previous studies have shown that some patients with cerebellar damage exhibit longer than usual reaction time delays when asked to make discrete, rapid movements (Beppu et al., 1987; Beppu et al., 1984; Day et al., 1998; Holmes, 1917; Vilis and Hore, 1980).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Kurtzer et al., 2013 studied cerebellar patients' ability to modulate long latency stretch responses that depend on knowledge of intersegmental dynamics of the arm.
source: Kurtzer et al., 2013 studied cerebellar patients' ability to modulate long latency stretch responses (i.e. EMG responses within 45–100 ms of a muscle stretch) that depend on knowledge of intersegmental dynamics of the arm.
evidence: This statement describes prior research findings.

claim: Cerebellar patient responses in the Kurtzer et al. study were found to have a lower gain and a slight delay in timing compared with controls.
source: Cerebellar patient responses were found to have a lower gain and a slight delay in timing compared with controls.
evidence: This statement describes findings from prior research.

claim: Cerebellar subjects can reweight which feedback modality to rely on (proprioception versus vision) depending on task demands.
source: These results combined suggest that cerebellar subjects can reweight which feedback modality to rely on (proprioception versus vision) depending on task demands, consistent with Block and Bastian, 2012
evidence: This is an interpretation of the combined results from this study and prior research.

claim: Previous work has proposed that the cerebellum might function in a manner consistent with a Smith Predictor.
source: While there is some controversy on this (Pélisson et al., 1986; Wolpert et al., 1998), previous work has proposed that the cerebellum might function in a manner consistent with a Smith Predictor (Miall et al., 1993).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A Smith Predictor is a control architecture that compensates for self-movement feedback delay.
source: Essentially, a Smith Predictor is a control architecture that compensates for self-movement feedback delay.
evidence: This is a definition from control theory.

claim: A Smith Predictor requires a simulation of the plant in order to predict sensory consequences of motor output, and a simulated delay that 'stores' the plant simulation for comparison with delayed feedback.
source: To achieve this requires a simulation of the plant in order to predict sensory consequences of motor output, and a simulated delay that 'stores' the plant simulation for comparison with delayed feedback.
evidence: This describes the components of a Smith Predictor from control theory.

claim: The patient model matches the simplified block diagram without a Smith Predictor and the age-matched control model matches the simplified block diagram with one.
source: Interestingly, upon simplification, we find the exact structures yielded by two of the top models (Best 5 Lowest Var and Best 4 Lowest Var): the patient model matches the simplified block diagram without a Smith Predictor and the age-matched control model matches the simplified block diagram which one.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling analysis comparing model structures to Smith Predictor architecture.

claim: An intact cerebellum may act in a manner qualitatively similar to a Smith Predictor.
source: This suggests that an intact cerebellum may act in a manner qualitatively similar to a Smith Predictor and that patients ability to perform such prediction is impaired.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the modeling results in the context of control theory.

claim: Patients' ability to perform prediction is impaired.
source: This suggests that an intact cerebellum may act in a manner qualitatively similar to a Smith Predictor and that patients ability to perform such prediction is impaired.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the modeling results.

claim: The apparent increased reliance on visual feedback seen in cerebellar patients may not be a compensatory mechanism at all.
source: Thus, the apparent increased reliance on visual feedback seen in cerebellar patients may not be a compensatory mechanism at all—perhaps all subjects rely on delayed visual feedback, but healthy subjects disguise the delay using predictions of future measurements of limb state.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the modeling results.

claim: All subjects rely on delayed visual feedback, but healthy subjects disguise the delay using predictions of future measurements of limb state.
source: perhaps all subjects rely on delayed visual feedback, but healthy subjects disguise the delay using predictions of future measurements of limb state.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the modeling results.

claim: Patients may simply lack the capability to disguise visual feedback delay and it is not that they compensate for their deficit by relying more on visual feedback.
source: Patients may simply lack this capability and it is not that they compensate for their deficit by relying more on visual feedback but instead that the loss of the sensory prediction and storage reveals the visual feedback delay inescapably present in both groups.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the modeling results.

claim: It was previously shown in weakly electric fish that target predictability can improve tracking performance.
source: Previously, it was shown in another species (weakly electric fish) that target predictability can indeed improve tracking performance, and it was hypothesized that this was based on an internal model of predictable reference motion (Roth et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Healthy human subjects show marked improvement in the single-sine (predictable) tracking task.
source: Here, we extend this to healthy human subjects who show marked improvement in the single-sine (predictable) tracking task.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiment 2.

claim: Cerebellar patients exhibit much more modest improvement in tracking predictable stimuli.
source: Cerebellar patients exhibit much more modest improvement in tracking predictable stimuli
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiment 2.

claim: Cerebellar patients may have impairment in both their own plant model predictions and predictions of external sensory references.
source: suggesting that they may have impairment in both their own plant model predictions and predictions of external sensory references (see Results, Experiment 2).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results from Experiment 2.

claim: A predictive model of action–perception could heighten perceptual sensitivity, making self-motion feedback more nuanced and precise.
source: recent evidence (Yon et al., 2018) suggests that a predictive model of action–perception could heighten perceptual sensitivity, making self-motion (in this case, cursor) feedback more nuanced and precise.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The success of the intervention provides support to the inertial mismatch theory.
source: Thus, the success of our intervention provides support to this inertial mismatch theory.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results from Experiment 3.

claim: Recent evidence based on the application of limb weights suggest that the inertial mismatch theory may be insufficient to explain dysmetria in multi-joint movements.
source: However, recent evidence based on the application of limb weights suggest that the inertial mismatch theory may be insufficient to explain dysmetria in multi-joint movements (Zimmet et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Feedback enhancement of multi-joint movements will likely require modifications of the simple acceleration-based controller tested in this paper.
source: Thus, feedback enhancement of multi-joint movements will likely require modifications of the simple acceleration-based controller tested in this paper.
evidence: This is a speculation about future work based on the limitations of the current approach.

claim: The 'best' acceleration-dependent feedback gain was patient specific even for the single-degree-of-freedom reaches tested.
source: Moreover, the 'best' acceleration-dependent feedback gain was patient specific even for the single-degree-of-freedom reaches tested for this study
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data in Experiment 3.

claim: Idiosyncrasies in each patient's motor control system may mandate patient-specific tuning.
source: suggesting that idiosyncrasies in each patient's motor control system (Kuling et al., 2017; Rincon-Gonzalez et al., 2011) may mandate patient-specific tuning.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The intervention does not attempt to reduce the variability of patient reaches.
source: Application of this visual feedback gain does not attempt to reduce the variability of patient reaches.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the intervention.

claim: The intervention does not completely eliminate the oscillations experienced by the subject after the first correction is made.
source: Secondly, our intervention does not completely eliminate the oscillations experienced by the subject after this first correction is made.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data in Experiment 3.

claim: The modeling work does not characterize or explain increased variability directly.
source: Moreover, our modeling work does not characterize or explain this increased variability directly.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the modeling approach.

claim: Adding a damping term to the feedback intervention might be able to address oscillatory behavior.
source: It is possible that adding a damping term to the feedback intervention might be able to address this oscillatory behavior.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential future improvements to the intervention.

claim: Cerebellar patients are capable of using their own intact visual feedback control system to make accurate reaches.
source: Our results provide an encouraging foundation for future studies because they show that cerebellar patients are capable of using their own intact visual feedback control system to make accurate reaches.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental results.

claim: Drug therapy for cerebellar ataxia is not currently viable.
source: These alternatives are especially important because drug therapy for cerebellar ataxia is not currently viable, leaving rehabilitative and assistive therapies alone as the primary means of treatment for these patients.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of treatment options for cerebellar ataxia.
